stories.title: Anthropic researcher's AI-generated proof of the Riemann hypothesis stuns mathematicians
stories.summary: Wired reports an Anthropic researcher used AI to produce a 17-million-line solution to the Riemann hypothesis, one of math's most famous open problems, though mathematicians say it will take months to understand the 'alien' proof.
stories.more: The article frames the development as a major moment for AI-assisted mathematics: an Anthropic researcher used AI to generate a solution to the Riemann hypothesis, a long-unsolved problem in number theory. The resulting proof reportedly runs to 17 million lines, far beyond what a human mathematician would typically produce or easily verify by hand. Wired describes the solution as 'alien,' reflecting how unfamiliar its structure and scale are to the field's usual proof style. The excerpt doesn't specify which AI model or method produced the proof, how it has been verified so far, or what the broader mathematical community's reaction has been beyond needing months to check it.

items.title: AI Solved Math’s Most Famous Problem. Now Humans Are Struggling to Understand It
items.excerpt: It will take mathematicians months to understand the “alien” 17-million-line solution an Anthropic researcher produced for the Riemann hypothesis.

stories.title: Researchers probe how frontier models act as robot-control policies
stories.summary: A new paper introduces Embo-Harness, a framework for systematically studying how frontier multimodal models serve directly as policies inside closed-loop robot-control harnesses, examining four components of such harnesses.
stories.more: Embo-Harness is presented as a framework for systematically studying how frontier multimodal models act as policies inside closed-loop robotic harnesses. The paper argues that despite impressive generalization in generating robot actions from observations and instructions, the design principles behind these harnesses and why they perform well remain unclear. The authors examine four components of the robotic harness, though the available excerpt cuts off before detailing what they are. It's not yet clear which models or robot platforms were used in the study, or what the findings imply for harness design going forward.

stories.title: New method trains code localizers on a fixer model's own judgment
stories.summary: A paper proposes Fixer-Guided Localization, which trains code localizers using scores from a frozen code-fixing model rather than ground-truth patch files, built on Gemma 4 E4B, without tests or reinforcement learning.
stories.more: The paper argues code localizers are typically trained to predict which files a reference patch edits, but that differs from the code a fixer actually needs to read to produce a fix. In Fixer-Guided Localization (FGL), a localizer proposes several candidate localizations, and a frozen fixer model scores each by how likely it is to produce a verified patch. The localizer is then trained on these scores via weighted supervised fine-tuning, without running tests or using reinforcement learning. The full pipeline is built on Gemma 4 E4B, though the excerpt cuts off before describing evaluation results or comparisons to other localization methods.

stories.title: WorldLeague benchmark tests AI systems on 60 physical robot tasks
stories.summary: WorldLeague is a new benchmark comparing AI systems on 60 shared simulated robot tasks, measuring progress toward each task's physical goal to test perception, memory, planning and action together.
stories.more: The benchmark responds to the fact that AI systems can already operate tools like Blender, follow instructions in video games, and manipulate objects with robot arms, but it's unclear what range of physical goals they can achieve autonomously. WorldLeague tests systems on 60 simulated robot tasks that each demand different combinations of perception, memory, planning, and action. Progress is measured by how close a system gets to each task's physical goal, rather than a simple pass/fail outcome. The excerpt cuts off before naming which AI systems were evaluated or how they performed.

stories.title: nanoAstra trains vision-language models for robot manipulation
stories.summary: nanoAstra is a new approach for training vision-language models as foundation models for robotic manipulation, combining semantic action modeling with supervised fine-tuning, after GPT-6 Astra's undisclosed robot-control results left the approach unreproducible.
stories.more: The paper notes that GPT-6 Astra has demonstrated strong generalization in robot control, but limited disclosure about its training has left the field without a clear path to reproduce those capabilities. nanoAstra aims to fill that gap by training vision-language models (VLMs) for generalizable manipulation. It represents robot behavior as semantic steps built from reusable, parameterized action primitives. Training combines semantic action modeling with capability-preserving supervised fine-tuning (CP-SFT), guided by explicit action primitives, though the excerpt cuts off before describing results or the benchmarks used to evaluate the approach.

stories.title: WeMM-Ecom brings multimodal LLMs tuned for WeChat e-commerce content

stories.more: The WeMM-Ecom family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model up to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. Training begins with two-stage continued pre-training that progressively raises the share of e-commerce data within a broader multimodal data mix, followed by further fine-tuning steps the excerpt cuts off before describing. The authors say the models reach state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales, not just on e-commerce tasks. stories.title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, an agent that reviews and approves PRs
stories.summary: Anthropic has launched Claude Ship, a beta tool in which AI agents review, fix, and approve pull request changes on their own according to a team's guidelines, automating more of the code-review workflow.
stories.more: Claude Ship is described as a new tool from Anthropic, currently in beta, that automatically reviews, corrects, and approves pull request suggestions in line with a team's established guidelines. The Decoder frames it as letting AI agents handle PR review end-to-end rather than just suggesting changes for a human to accept. The excerpt doesn't detail how teams configure their guidelines, what happens when the agent is unsure, or how much human oversight remains in the approval step. It's also unclear from the available text when Claude Ship will move beyond beta or which other Anthropic products it integrates with.

stories.title: Young people say AI optimism is straining their holiday conversations
stories.summary: Wired reports that young people anxious about their job prospects are increasingly frustrated with pro-AI parents, worried that differing views on AI will make Thanksgiving gatherings tense this year.
stories.more: The piece centers on a generational divide: young people who are anxious about how AI could affect their career prospects say they're growing frustrated with parents who are more optimistic about the technology. That gap in attitudes, the article says, risks making holiday gatherings tense. The excerpt doesn't name specific surveys, data, or individuals quoted, so it's unclear how widespread this sentiment is beyond the anecdotal framing.

items.title: Don’t Bring Up AI if You Want to Enjoy Your Thanksgiving
items.excerpt: Young people anxious about their futures say they’re increasingly frustrated with their pro-AI parents. They’re worried it’s going to make holiday gatherings very tense.
